### page_1
Paleo- and Mesoproterozoic dyke swarms at Lake Ladoga area,
NW Russia – paleomagnetic studies
S. Mertanen
Geological Survey of Finland, Espoo, Finland
O. Eklund & A. Shebanov
University of Turku, Turku, Finland
D. Frank-Kamenetsky
State Company Mineral, St.Petersburg, Russia
T. Vasilieva
Geological Institute of RAS, Moscow, Russia
ABSTRACT: New paleomagnetic and rock magnetic data are presented from Paleoproterozoic
1.8 Ga shoshonitic intrusions and associated NW-SE trending lamprophyre dykes, and from
undated NE-SW trending dolerite dykes at Lake Ladoga area in NW Russia. The shoshonitic
intrusions and lamprophyre dykes are suggested to carry a primary 1.8 Ga remanent
magnetization residing in titanomagnetite. In addition, they carry a partial remagnetization
component that probably resides in titanomaghemite. The dolerite dykes show a single
remanence component that is thought to be a primary thermoremanent magnetization. The
paleomagnetic pole positions obtained from this component are Mesoproterozoic in age (ca.
1.54 Ga). This age corresponds to that of the Salmi rapakivi massif that is found near the study
area. Thus, we interpret this magnetic component to be associated with widespread thermal and
magmatic events associated with rapakivi magmatism and emplacement of associated dolerite
dykes. Such events may also be responsible for the partial remagnetization of the shoshonites
and lamprophyres.
1 INTRODUCTION
The Lake Ladoga area in NW Russia forms a key location of the Fennoscandian Shield in that it
preserves a record of most of the significant geological events that the shield has experienced
from the Archean to the Paleozoic. The main part of the studied area was formed during the
Paleoproterozoic Svecofennian orogeny at ca. 1.9-1.8 Ga. Later on the Svecofennian rocks were
intruded by Mesoproterozoic ca. 1.65-1.53 Ga rapakivi granites and associated dykes and
volcanic rocks. In this study, we present paleomagnetic results from 1.8 Ga post-collisional
shoshonitic intrusions (Eklund et al. 1998) and coeval lamprophyre dykes and from dolerite
dykes that are thought to be related to the 1.54 Ga rapakivi granites. Geochemical, petrological
and isotope age data obtained from the same sites as paleomagnetic data will be reported
elsewhere (see Shebanov & Eklund 2005, Shebanov et al. 2006). The main aim of the
paleomagnetic studies was to isolate the primary remanent magnetizations of the 1.8 Ga dykes
and intrusions in order to obtain new reliable data for constructing the Fennoscandian plate
movement, and to facilitate studies on the Paleoproterozoic supercontinents. The other aim was
to study possible effects of the intrusion of the Mesoproterozoic rapakivi granites on the
remanent magnetization of Paleoproterozoic rocks.
2 GEOLOGY AND SAMPLING
The area west of Lake Ladoga in northwestern Russia (Fig. 1) is mainly composed of
Paleoproterozoic ca. 1880-1975 Ma tonalitic migmatites and granitoids (Konopelko & Eklund
2003, Konopelko et al. 2005). The northen part of the area is delinated by Archean (more than

Figure 1. Location of the study area and sampling sites. Paleomagnetic results were obtained from the
shoshonitic intrusions of Vuoksa (VK), Ojajärvi (OJ) and Elisenvaara (EL and ES), from the NW-SE
trending lamprophyre dykes of Ivan's Island (IV) and Reuskula (RE) and from the NE-SW trending

2.65 Ga) and early Paleoproterozoic (ca. 2.0 Ga) rock types (Koistinen et al. 2001) and the
1547-1530 Ma (Amelin et al. 1997) Salmi rapakivi massif. In the southwestern part of the study
area, the 1.65-1.62 Ga (Vaasjoki 1977) Wyborg rapakivi batholith is found.
In the post-collisional stage of the Svecofennian orogeny at ca. 1.8 Ga, the Svecofennian
basement was intruded by shoshonitic magmas, ranging in composition from lamprophyres to
granites. The shoshonitic intrusions represent magmas derived from enriched litospheric mantle,
emplaced at upper crustal levels (Eklund et al. 1998, Konopelko & Eklund 2003). The
intrusions form a conspicuous belt extending from Lake Ladoga area in NW Russia to Åland
archipelago in SW Finland (Eklund et al. 1998). Paleomagnetic studies have now been carried
out on three dated shoshonitic intrusions at Lake Ladoga area (Fig. 1); the Vuoksa (1802±17
Ma, U-Pb, zircon, Konopelko & Ivanikov 1996), Ojajärvi (1800-1805 Ma, K-Ar, amphibole,
Ivanikov et al. 1996) and Elisenvaara (1800±6 Ma, U-Pb, zircon, Konopelko & Vaasjoki 2002,
pers. comm.) intrusions. Paleomagnetic results from the intrusions are reported in more detail in
Mertanen et al. (2005) and the main conclusions are briefly described in this paper.
The shoshonitic intrusions are genetically related to the lamprophyre dykes as they may be
fractionated from lamprophyric melts (Eklund et al. 1998, Konopelko et al. 1998, Konopelko &
Eklund, 2003). At least 7 lamprophyre dykes are presently known in the area (Vasilieva et al.
2002, Vasilieva & Frank-Kamenetsky 2003). Figure 1 shows schematically the locations of the
dykes. U-Pb ages of the lamprophyres were determined on zircons with SIMS (Shebanov &
Eklund 2005, Shebanov et al. 2006). Dating was carried out on three dykes in the Kalto Island,
and on dykes of Ivan's Island (IV), Reuskula (RE) and Meijeri (Fig. 1). Isotopic dating of the
lamprophyres was problematic because they commonly contained zircons that had been
inherited from an Archean source. In the dyke of the Ivan's Island, no emplacement age was

### page_3
obtained at all, as all the studied zircons are inherited and give only Archean ages. In the
Reuskula lamprophyre the upper intersect gives an age of 2.75 Ga and the lower, an age of 1.8-
1.7 Ga. The Meijeri dyke gives a population of inherited zircon with an age of 2.65 Ga, and an
older Svecofennian age. The Kalto lamprophyres were most thoroughly analysed (4 dykes, 45
zircons) and they show different ages: 1) 1862±5 Ma, 2) 1896±7 Ma for a zircon core, and 3)
1777±33 Ma for the rim (Shebanov & Eklund 2005, Shebanov et al. 2006).
For paleomagnetic studies, samples were taken from the Vuoksa (VK) intrusion (9 samples),
the Ojajärvi (OJ) intrusion (19 samples) and from the two pipe like bodies of the Elisenvaara
(EL and ES) intrusion (11 samples). Seven lamprophyre dykes were sampled; three dykes in the
Kalto Island, the Ivan's Island dyke (IV), the Reuskula (RE) and Meijeri dykes and a dyke that
cross cuts the Elisenvaara intrusion. Unfortunately, the Kalto, Meijeri and Elisenvaara dykes did
not carry stable remanent magnetizations. Consequently, paleomagnetic results were obtained
only from two lamprophyres, the Ivan's Island dyke (18 samples) and the Reuskula dyke (5
samples). The trend of the lamprophyres is 112-115 . The 60 cm wide Reuskula dyke is
vertical, but the 40-60 cm wide Ivan's Island dyke has a dip of 40 that is regarded to represent
the original orientation acquired during the emplacement of the dyke (Vasilieva et al. 2002).
We also obtained paleomagnetic samples from three dykes (LA, LB and LC) from an undated
dolerite dyke swarm (Fig. 1). On the basis of geochemical composition and the presence of
anorthositic xenoliths and plagioclase phenocrysts, we consider these dykes to be genetically
associated with the Mesoproterozoic rapakivi granites. The trend of the dykes is 75-60 and they
are subvertical or vertical (dip 80-90 ). The biggest of the dykes, the coarse grained dyke LB
(12 samples) has a width of ca. 40 m, while the narrowest dyke LA (7 samples) has a width of
30-40 cm. Dykes LB and LC (10 samples) are mostly eroded away, but sampling could be
carried out on chilled margins and on a restricted area in the center of dyke LB.
In order to carry out baked contact tests for the intrusions and the dykes, samples were taken
also from the Svecofennian host gneisses. Unfortunately, the host rocks are very weakly
magnetized and do not yield stable paleomagnetic results.
3 METHODS
Density and magnetic susceptibility were measured for all specimens before palaeomagnetic
measurements. Remanence measurements were made using a 2G-Enterprises SQUID
magnetometer and a Schoenstedt magnetometer. Demagnetizations were done both by
alternating field (AF) up to peak field of 160 mT and thermally up to peak temperature of
680ºC. Mineralogical alterations were observed by monitoring the magnetic susceptibility after
each thermal step. Remanence components were visually inspected by Zijderveld diagrams
(Leino 1991, Zijderveld 1967) and the components were identified using principal component
analysis (Kirshcvink 1980).
Magnetic carriers were identified by thermomagnetic analysis by using an Agico CS2-KLY2
Kappabridge, applying stepwise heating up to 700ºC. In order to further characterize the
magnetic mineralogy, Lowrie-Fuller tests (Lowrie & Fuller 1971) were performed on selected
specimens. The samples were first stepwise demagnetized in alternating fields up to 160 mT,
and then given an anhysteretic remanent magnetization (ARM) in a peak AF of 200 mT and a
biasing field of 0.1 mT. The ARM was then progressively AF demagnetized in peak fields up to
160 mT. The specimens were then pulse magnetized in a Molspin pulse magnetizer in fifteen
steps between 25 and 1500 mT to produce SIRM. It was then progressively AF demagnetized in
peak fields up to 100 or 160 mT.
4 ROCK MAGNETIC AND PALEOMAGNETIC RESULTS
4.1 Rock magnetism
Isothermal magnetization measurements for dykes and shoshonitic intrusions (Fig. 2) show a
rapid increase up to about 200 mT and a total saturation well below 1 T, indicating magnetite or
a low titanium titanomagnetite as the remanence carrier. Lowrie-Fuller tests (Lowrie & Fuller

1971) show that in all rock types the remanence resides mainly in SD or PSD particles (Fig. 3).
However, in samples from dyke IV, RE and OA, the ARM is weaker than IRM to AF
demagnetization in high fields, suggesting that the remanence is carried by a mixture of finer
SD/PSD and coarser MD grains.
Thermomagnetic analyses (magnetic susceptibility versus temperature, k-T) are shown in
Figure 4. K-T curves for the Vuoksa and Ojajärvi shoshonitic intrusions (Fig. 4a,b) yield
reversible heating and cooling curves with a Curie point of ca. 580°C, implying the presence of
pure magnetite. However, the Elisenvaara intrusions (Fig. 4c,d) that are compositionally more
heterogeneous than the Vuoksa and Ojajärvi intrusions, comprising a differentation series from
ultramafic variations (Fig. 4c) to more acid rocks (Fig. 4d) show strongly irreversible heating
and cooling curves, indicating mineralogical alterations during heating. Likewise, the
lamprophyre and dolerite dykes (Fig. 4e-h) show conspicious increase of intensity in the cooling
curves indicating considerable creation of magnetite during heating. In both specimens from the
lamprophyre dykes IV and RE (Fig. 4e,f) there is a very slight decrease of intensity in the
heating curves at the temperature of ca. 350ºC which may be an indication of the occurrence of
titanomaghemite, titanomagnetite or pyrrhotite.

and Koenigsberger ratios (Q-values) are given in Table 1.

4.2.2 Lamprophyre dykes
Thermal demagnetization was more effective in isolating the characteristic components of the
two magnetically stable lamprophyre dykes IV and RE (Fig. 1) than AF methods. By applying
thermal demagnetization, two consistent remanence directions were isolated in all samples
(Table 2 and Fig. 8b), while AF demagnetization mostly produced spurious directions which

4.2.3 Dolerite dykes
The characteristic remanence component of the dolerite dykes show southwesterly declinations
and shallow positive inclinations (Table 2, Figs. 7 and 8b) which are close to the direction of the
S component of the lamprophyres and shoshonites. Like the lamprophyres, the dolerite dykes
R
were more effectively demagnetized by thermal demagnetization than by AF methods, which in
most cases showed odd behaviours. However, part of the AF demagnetizes samples showed
extremely stable behaviour with a single component (see Fig. 7c). Dykes LA and LC have
slightly lower inclinations than dyke LB. Dyke LB is 40 m wide and has cooled more slowly
than the narrower dykes LA and LC, thus allowing some alteration to take place in the late
stages of cooling. Thermal demagnetization of dyke LB indicate the presence of two magnetic
phases that, based on unblocking temperatures, are probably low-titanium titanomagnetite
(demagnetized between 520-570 C) and titanomaghemite (330-370 C). In the marginal parts of
the dyke the remanence is unblocked within the whole temperature range of 330-570 C (see
specimen LB21-4B, Fig. 7) thus evidencing that the maghemitization took place during cooling

5 DISCUSSION
In order to constrain the ages of magnetizations, paleomagnetic poles were calculated for the
characteristic remanence components A and S (Table 2, Fig. 9). Although paleomagnetic field
tests, like baked contact tests, were succesfull neither for the intrusions nor for the dykes due to
weak remanence intensities and instability of remanence of the host gneisses, we believe that
remanence component A is the primary remanence of the shoshonites and the lamprophyres.
Since the intrusions were emplaced at upper crustal levels (Eklund et al. 1998, Konopelko &
Eklund 2003) where the cooling of magma is relatively rapid, the U-Pb ages can be correlated
with the timing of the remanence.
The shoshonitic intrusions are dated precisely (see section 2) and show ages of ca. 1.8 Ga.
Also the SIMS datings of most of the lamprophyres give interpretable results (Shebanov &
Eklund 2005, Shebanov et al. 2006). However, the age of some lamprophyres was poorly
determined. The dating for the Ivan's Island dyke contained only inherited zircons with Archean
ages, and no Svecofennian ages. However, based on the correspondence of the paleomagnetic
poles from the shoshonites and the lamprophyres (Fig. 9a), both the Ivan's Island dyke and the
Reuskula dyke are probably about the same age as the shoshonites. The paleomagnetic poles of
component A are close to the known 1.88-1.83 Ga key poles of the Fennoscandian Shield. The
1.88 Ga key pole is obtained from gabbroic intrusions in central Finland and the 1.83 Ga key
pole from the Haukivesi lamprophyre dykes in central Finland (see Buchan et al. 2000, Pesonen
et al. 2003 for references). The result thus implies that during the Svecofennian orogeny, no
significant plate movement took place. However, as the poles from the shoshonites show a little
higher latitudes than the 1.88 and 1.83 Ga key poles, it is possible that at the post-collisional
stage of the orogeny, the shield had moved to slightly higher paleolatitudes (Mertanen et al.,
2003, 2005).
Poles from the secondary component S (Fig. 9a) plot among the 1.63-1.54 Ga key poles of
the Fennoscandian Shield (see Buchan et al. 2000, Pesonen et al. 2003). The key poles are
obtained from the diabase and quartz porphyry dykes associated with the rapakivi granites of the
Åland and Onas rapakivi granites in southern Finland. Based on pole positions, which are

### page_10
mainly based on data from a few samples, the exact age for pole S cannot be determined.
However, the position of poles clearly indicates that magnetization S was acquired during
Mesopropterozoic. Especially, the better defined poles from the Elisenvaara intrusion (ES) and
from the Ivan's Island dyke (IV) are in agreement with the 1.54 Ga key pole of the
Fennoscandian Shield (Fig. 9). The age of the Salmi rapakivi massif (Fig. 1) is 1.53-1.55 Ga,
and, thus it represents a possible source for the remagnetization event. The Elisenvaara body
was evidently totally remagnetized during the emplacement of the Salmi rapakivi massif (Fig.
1).
For the dolerite dykes (Fig. 9b) it is implied that remanence component S represents the
primary magnetization of the dykes, although no field tests are available. The poles from the
dolerite dykes compare rather well, although not fully matching with the 1.63 - 1.54 Ga key
poles of the Fennoscandian Shield. Based on correspondence of pole S from the dolerite dykes
to the key poles and on the basis of their compositional and petrological resemblance to the
rapakivi granites, it is therefore likely that the dolerite dykes represent magmatism associated
with the emplacement of the rapakivi granites. Emplacement of the dolerite dykes form a
plausible additional source for the partial remagnetization of the 1.8 Ga old shoshonitic
intrusions and lamprophyre dykes.
The paleomagnetic results from northewestern Russia document the vast effect of the
rapakivi magmatism into the adjacent rocks. The Mesoproterozoic remagnetization was isolated
as a partial overprint in rocks that are not in close proximity to the rapakivi granites. It is
therefore implied that at Lake Ladoga area, the thermal effect of the rapakivi granites may have
extended to the intermediate areas between the rapakivi batholiths. Previous paleomagnetic
studies on shear and fault zones in southern Finland (Mertanen et al. 2004) have also
demonstrated a reactivation and partial remagnetization of the crust during emplacement of the
rapakivi granites. In this area the emplacement of the coeval dolerite dykes probably formed
another source for reactivation.

Figure 9. Paleomagnetic poles (VGP's) from a) the shoshonitic intrusions VK and OJ (circles), the
lamprophyre dykes RE and IV (triangels) and from b) the dolerite dykes LA, LB and LC (squares). The
Precambrian key poles of the Fennoscandian Shield are shown as crosses with dashed A95 confidence
cones and ages (Ma). In a) the shaded A95 confidence cones are shown for the mean A poles VK, OJ,
RE and IV that are regarded as primary, ca. 1800 Ma old, and for the mean S poles ES and IV that are
regarded as secondary, ca. 1540 Ma old. The secondary poles RE, OJ and VK plot among the key poles of
the ages of 1630-1540 Ga and were calculated for comparison, althoug the remanence component was
obtained only in a few samples (therefore, no A95 confidence cones are shown). In b) the A95 confidence
cone is shown for the mean pole from dykes LA, LB and LC, and is regarded as 1630-1540 Ma old.

### page_11
6 CONCLUSIONS
Paleomagnetic results from well-dated 1.8 Ga shoshonitic intrusions are in accord with the
results from the genetically related lamprophyre dykes. Both the shoshonitic intrusions and the
lamprophyre dykes yield a stable remanence component (A) which is regarded to represent the
primary remanent magnetization acquired ca. 1.8 Ga. In both rock types the A component is
demagnetized below 580 C indicating magnetite as the remanence carrier. The paleomagnetic
poles obtained from these rocks are close to the 1.88 and 1.83 Ga key poles of the
Fennoscandian Shield, thus indicating that no extensive plate movement took place in the post-
collisional stage of the Svecofennian orogeny.
The shoshonites and lamprophyres carry a secondary component (S) as an ancient overprint.
It is demagnetized below 370 C thus suggesting that the remanence may reside in
titanomaghemite. Comparison of the pole position to the key paleomagnetic poles, implies that
the S remanence was acquired at ca. 1.54 Ga. The age of remanence is in agreement with the
age of the nearby Salmi rapakivi granite massif. It is therefore concluded that the effect of the
rapakivi magmatism has extended to the areas where no intrusions occur.
Another dyke swarm of undated dolerite dykes yield a corresponding remanence component
S as what was obtained in the shoshonities and lamprophyres. In the dolerite dykes this
remanence component is regarded to be of primary origin, acquired during cooling of the dykes
at about the same time as the rapakivi intrusions. The emplacement of the dolerite dyke swarm
thus forms another source for the partial remagnetization of the shoshonites and lamprophyres.

Paleomagnetic studies at Lake Ladoga area were initiated in the SVEKALAPKO project by
Nikolay Philippov who was the first to suggest paleomagnetic investigations on shoshonitic
intrusions in the area. The earliest field works of SM were carried out with him, Vasili Ivanikov,
Vladimir Bogatchev and Valery Litvinenko who are greatly acknowledged both for their
guidance in the field and for the discussions about the geology of shoshonites. Vasili Ivachenko,
Peik Aura, Gustav Westerlund and Viveca Lindqvist are thanked for their help in the field.
Matti Leino is acknowledged for his assistance in the paleomagnetic laboratory of GTK and
Markku Kääriä and Tuula Laine for making the paleomagnetic measurements. Stephen Harlan
and Sten-Åke Elming are acknowledged for their constructive suggestions and criticism which
significantly helped to improve the manuscript. TV was supported by a grant: RFBR 04-05-
64554.
